subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
bigPicture: A negative ΔH is not the whole story: reactions also tend to spread matter and energy out (entropy). Gibbs energy combines the two, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and its sign tells you whether a change is thermodynamically spontaneous at a given temperature, and how far an equilibrium lies.

keyIdeas.cue: What is entropy and how do you predict and calculate ΔS?
keyIdeas.answer: Entropy, S, measures how dispersed matter and energy are: S(gas) ≫ S(liquid) > S(solid). ΔS is positive when gas moles increase, a solid dissolves, or something melts or boils. ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants), in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Elements do not have S = 0.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you use ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵?
keyIdeas.answer: Convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (÷ 1000) so units match ΔH (kJ mol⁻¹). T in kelvin. The booklet also lists ΔGf⦵ values, which you can use like ΔHf: ΔG = ΣΔGf(products) − ΣΔGf(reactants).

keyIdeas.cue: When is a reaction spontaneous, and at what temperature does it switch?
keyIdeas.answer: Spontaneous (at constant pressure) when ΔG < 0. ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0: always. ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0: never. Same signs: temperature decides; switch-over at T = ΔH/ΔS (ΔG = 0). ΔG includes both the system's entropy change and the surroundings' (via heat transferred, −ΔH/T). 'Spontaneous' says nothing about rate.

keyIdeas.cue: How does ΔG relate to equilibrium?
keyIdeas.answer: As a reaction proceeds towards equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and reaches zero at equilibrium. ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q; at equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, so ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K. ΔG⦵ < 0 → K > 1 (products favoured); ΔG⦵ > 0 → K < 1.

keyTerms.def: Measure of the dispersal of matter and energy in a system; J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
ΔH − TΔS; negative for a spontaneous change at constant T and P.
Thermodynamically favourable; can happen without continuous outside energy (may still be slow).

workedExamples.title: Switch-over temperature
workedExamples.prompt: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g): ΔH⦵ = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS⦵ = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Is it spontaneous at 298 K? Above which temperature does it become spontaneous?
workedExamples.answer: Not at 298 K; spontaneous above ≈ 1106 K (≈ 833 °C).

workedExamples.title: ΔG⦵ to K
workedExamples.prompt: A reaction has ΔG⦵ = −10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Calculate K.

misconceptions.right: Spontaneity is about thermodynamics; a spontaneous reaction can be extremely slow (diamond → graphite).

misconceptions.wrong: You can use ΔS in J with ΔH in kJ directly.
misconceptions.right: Convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ first.
Not if ΔS is negative and T is high enough that −TΔS outweighs ΔH.

paper1A.stem: Which change has the largest increase in entropy?
paper1A.why: Liquid to gas is the biggest increase in dispersal.

paper1A.stem: A reaction has ΔH = −50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. When is it spontaneous?
paper1A.why: ΔG < 0 while TΔS (in kJ) is smaller than 50, i.e. T < 500 K.

paper1A.stem: What does ΔG⦵ > 0 tell you about K?
paper1A.why: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, so ln K < 0.

paper1B.data: Booklet-style data (S⦵ / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): C₂H₄(g) +220; H₂(g) +131; C₂H₆(g) +230.
paper1B.prompt: Calculate ΔS⦵ for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ and explain its sign.
paper1B.answer: 230 − (220 + 131) = −121 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; negative because 2 mol gas become 1 mol gas.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.
